title: Get the Leadership Recognition You Deserve—Through Impact, Not Just Effort 2026
author: Kurt Mueller
source: Rookie to Pro: The Hidden Side of Leadership (kurtmueller.substack.com), November 13,
summary: Kurt Mueller argues that when recognition or advancement stalls, the problem is often not a leader's capability but how that capability is applied to the situation at hand. Every leader has a preferred response to challenges, and those habits become liabilities when they do not match what a situation requires. He gives three examples: a presentation-first meeting style that misses unspoken stakeholder concerns, team protection that creates delays for downstream departments, and an accommodating style that hides necessary trade-offs. His fix, which he calls Situational Alignment, asks what the situation requires, how your normal response might help or hinder, and what adjustment would work better, then practising and learning from the result. The point is that measurable impact, not effort, gives a leader something to show when seeking advancement, and that this development need not wait on an employer.
points: A leader's default style is a strength until it stops matching what the situation demands, and then it quietly blocks results.
Before advocating a solution, ask stakeholders what they see as the biggest obstacles to success.
Protecting your team can damage the wider value chain, so ask who depends on your deliverables and what they need.
Accommodating every request makes trade-offs invisible; make priorities, timing and deferrals explicit.
Situational Alignment is three questions plus practice: what the situation needs, how your habit helps or hinders, and what adjustment to try.
quotes: Every leader develops a preferred way of responding to challenges. It’s shaped by experience, personal values, previous successes, and sometimes the lessons learned from a difficult boss.
Your leadership capability may not be the problem. How you’re applying it to the situations you encounter may be.
Your instinct is to explain your recommendation more thoroughly. Unfortunately, what the situation really needs is active listening and an opportunity to uncover those concerns.
But another department depends on your team’s deliverables. Your protection inadvertently creates delays and frustration downstream.
Your willingness to accommodate everyone is creating uncertainty about what matters most.
None requires abandoning your leadership values or personality. Instead, they require recognizing what the situation demands and intentionally selecting a more effective leadership response.
Then comes the essential ingredient: put your adjustment into practice, observe the results, and learn from the experience.
